title: Why your brain procrastinates
summary: Procrastination is often less about laziness and more about mood repair: we dodge tasks that feel bad right now, even when it costs us later.
evidenceNote: The emotion-regulation view of procrastination is well supported, but procrastination has several causes. 'Make the first step tiny' is a practical strategy rather than a single proven cure.

scenes.text: Research suggests it's often about mood: we avoid tasks that feel boring, confusing or threatening right now.
Your brain weighs two very different rewards.

left.label: Now
left.text: Instant relief: a scroll, a snack, a tidy desk

right.label: Later
right.text: A finished task, weeks away and abstract

scenes.text: That's why checking your phone feels easier than opening the document you've been dreading.
Shrink the first step until it barely feels like work: open the file, write one sentence.
Don't aim to finish. Aim to start.

sources.title: Procrastination and the priority of short-term mood regulation
